summary: Describes how the Server-based Certificate Validation Protocol (SCVP) can be used together with Evidence Record Syntax to prove, long afterward, that a signature or certificate path was valid. SCVP lets a server validate a certificate path for a client and can answer for a time in the past, which helps with long-term archives.

eli5.summary: A signed paper can be checked years later, even after the stamp on it expired. This uses a trusted helper to say the stamp was good back then, and keeps that note as proof.

questions: how to validate a certificate after it expires
subtitle: How a certificate validation server can hand back long-term proof records for the certificates and revocation data it used.

tldr.problem: Checking a signature many years later is hard: needed certificates and revocation data may be gone or expired, and the algorithms used may no longer be secure.
tldr.mechanism: New SCVP WantBack identifiers let a client ask the server for an Evidence Record Syntax (ERS) evidence record that covers each piece of certification path or revocation data in the response.
tldr.outcome: A client can validate an archived, signed object with SCVP evidence records alongside it, without storing full verification data with every object.

facts.label: Evidence record covers
facts.value: The value field, not tag and length

today: RFC 5276 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2008. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Long-Term Validation Problem
sections.content:
Verifying a digital signature means building and validating a certification path from the signer's certificate to a trusted public key. Doing this many years after signing is harder: some PKI artifacts may no longer be available, some may have expired, and the cryptographic algorithms or keys may no longer give the desired security.

The Server-Based Certificate Validation Protocol (SCVP, RFC 5055) lets a client delegate path construction and validation to a server, including for a time in the past. It does not provide long-term non-repudiation information. The Evidence Record Syntax (ERS, RFC 4998) does preserve material over long periods, by periodically re-signing it with newer keys and stronger algorithms. This RFC joins the two.
sections.eli5: Old documents are hard to check because the people and stamps that vouched for them may be gone. This RFC connects a checking helper to a record-keeping system so the proof survives.

sections.title: Concept of Operations
sections.content:
Active SCVP servers see many of the PKI artifacts a PKI generates. By storing and preserving them, a server can answer certificate status queries over very long periods. Servers may even seek out PKI information to preserve when no query is made.

Clients tell an SCVP server what to return by including zero or more Object Identifiers (OIDs) in the request. This RFC defines new OIDs so a client can ask for an evidence record covering specific types of information: end entity certificates, certification paths from an end entity certificate to a trust anchor, certification paths from an intermediate certificate to a trust anchor, and revocation information. One more OID asks for evidence records for everything requested.

Because the server signs its response, that signature can secure the transmission of trust anchors included in evidence records. Clients then do not need extra trust relationships with long-term archive (LTA) servers.
sections.eli5: You tell the helper which kinds of proof you want, using special code words. The helper signs the whole package so you can trust what is inside.

sections.title: Verifying an Archived Object
sections.content:
The RFC lists the steps to verify a signed object kept in a long-term archive that speaks LTAP (the Long-term Archive Protocol):

  1. The client retrieves the signed archived data object from the LTA using LTAP.
  2. The client sends an SCVP request to validate the signer's certificate at the time of interest, with WantBacks for evidence records covering the PKI artifacts needed.
  3. The SCVP server returns the status as of that time plus the requested evidence records.
  4. The client processes the response, determines the status and verifies the evidence records.
  5. The client verifies the signatures in the archived object using the now validated signer's certificate.

Keeping certification path information separate from the archived data lets the archive store objects more efficiently, since complete verification information need not accompany each one. Verifiers can reuse the same path information for many objects of similar vintage.
sections.eli5: First you fetch the old document. Then you ask the helper if the signer's stamp was good back then. The helper answers with proof, you check the proof, and only then do you trust the signature.

sections.title: Requests and Responses
sections.content:
A client asks for evidence records by putting one of these OIDs in the wantBack field of a CVRequest: id-swb-ers-best-cert-path, id-swb-ers-partial-cert-path, id-swb-ers-pkc-cert, id-swb-ers-revocation-info or id-swb-ers-all. A separate id-swb-partial-cert-path asks for a partial path from the CA that issued the end entity certificate through a trust anchor, so the result is a CertBundle without the end entity certificate.

For each id-swb-ers OID except id-swb-ers-all, an EvidenceRecord covering the matching information comes back as a replyWantBack. With id-swb-ers-all, an EvidenceRecordWantBacks structure carries one evidence record per information item.

The response MUST include both the requested information and its evidence record. The record MUST be calculated over the value of the value field of the matching replyWantBack, without the tag and length bytes. For id-swb-ers-pkc-cert it is calculated over the cert field of the CertReply.

If the server cannot supply a requested evidence record, it MUST still return a replyWantBack of that type with an empty (zero length) value field.
sections.eli5: You ask for a document and, next to it, a certificate of proof for it. If the helper has no proof to give, it sends an empty envelope so you know.

sections.title: The WantBacks
sections.content:
Each evidence record WantBack needs the WantBack for the object it covers in the same request. If that is missing, the server MUST indicate wantBackUnsatisfied in the ReplyStatus. Responses containing an evidence record WantBack MUST also contain the paired one.

  • id-swb-ers-best-cert-path pairs with id-swb-best-cert-path and covers a complete certification path, from end entity to trust anchor. The record is calculated over the returned CertBundle.
  • id-swb-ers-partial-cert-path pairs with id-swb-partial-cert-path. Servers can save storage by keeping records only for partial paths. The end entity certificate could instead be included in the archived data object.
  • id-swb-ers-pkc-cert pairs with id-swb-pkc-cert and covers one certificate, so clients can omit the signer's certificate from the archived object.
  • id-swb-ers-revocation-info pairs with id-swb-revocation-info. A sequence of evidence records is returned, one per element. Revocation information may be CRLs or OCSP responses, and cumulative CRLs may be generated to simplify record maintenance.
  • id-swb-ers-all asks for records for every item returned in replyWantBacks. Each EvidenceRecordWantBack holds a targetWantBack OID and an optional evidenceRecord. There MUST be a one-to-one correspondence with the other reply objects, and a missing record is shown by leaving evidenceRecord absent.
sections.eli5: Each kind of proof comes paired with the thing it proves, like a receipt stapled to a purchase. You cannot ask for a receipt without also asking for the item.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security issues specific to SCVP are in RFC 5055, and those specific to ERS are in RFC 4998. This RFC adds a point about trust anchors.

The signature on an SCVP response carrying ERS structures must be verified with a public key the relying party trusts. The response may contain trust anchors for verifying interior layers of an ERS structure, and the server's signature protects them. The relying party may use those anchors or ignore them in favor of anchors obtained out of band. Relying parties SHOULD ignore trust anchors in unsigned SCVP responses.
sections.eli5: Only believe the helper's package if it carries the helper's trusted signature. An unsigned package could have been tampered with.
